question: Since at least 2016 raw sewage has been discharged into the sea in Newport, County Mayo, Ireland due to the inadequate wastewater infrastructure. The effluent is discharged into Clew Bay, which is a Special Area of Conservation and a designated shellfish area. This has raised serious environmental and public health concerns in the local community.

Uisce Éireann, the national utility responsible for water services in Ireland, cannot give a definitive date for the upgrade of the Newport sewerage scheme and the construction of a new wastewater treatment plant.

They have stated that in the optimistic scenario where the necessary licences, consents and permissions are granted for each stage without any objections, planning appeals, legal challenges or undue delays, then a wastewater treatment plant of this kind could be completed in five to seven years. 1.
Is the Commission concerned about the impact these discharges are having on the Special Area of Conservation in Clew Bay?
Is the Commission concerned about the timescale given by Uisce Éireann for the upgrade of the wastewater infrastructure?
Does this contravene EU environmental legislation and will the Commission consider raising this matter with the Irish authorities?
answer: 1. As regards Special Areas of Conservation, the Habitats Directive (1) requires any project that might significantly affect a Natura 2000 site to be assessed on its conservation objectives (2). Authorities may agree to the project if it will not adversely affect the site’s integrity.

Member States must take steps to avoid deterioration of natural habitats and significant disturbance of designated species, whose protection regime must be respected, according to guidance (3), (4), (5). 2. The timeline for improving Newport’s wastewater infrastructure might not be optimal.

However, the Urban Wastewater Treatment Directive (UWWTD) (6) includes limited obligations for agglomerations below 2 000 population equivalents, like Newport (below 700). Since Member States do not have to report on them, the Commission has no automatic follow-up role.

However, the revised UWWTD (7), recently agreed by the co-legislators, expands the scope of application to cover smaller agglomeration above 1 000 population equivalents. 3. Without prejudice to the Commission’s role as guardian of the Treaties, Member States are primarily responsible for compliance with their obligations under EU law.

Under the Water Framework Directive (8), Ireland reported high ecological and good chemical status for Newport Bay in its 2nd River Basin Management Plan (RBMP) (9), and good ecological status in Clew Bay. Ireland has not reported the 3rd RBMPs. A letter of formal notice was sent in February 2023, followed by a reasoned opinion in September 2023.

In February 2024 (10) the Commission referred the case to the Court of Justice of the EU. The Irish RBMPs will be assessed when submitted by the Irish authorities. The Commission will monitor the situation and may decide to take appropriate action.

Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7-50.
